formatIntel.summary: Not a LeetCode loop. Palantir tests how you handle undefined scope, unfamiliar code, and unfamiliar systems. Know Foundry (commercial) from Gotham (government) — surface-level answers about 'interesting problems' get filtered at the screen.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.scoring: Whether you can tell Foundry from Gotham and say something specific about why Palantir
rounds.prep: One concrete sentence on why this company, not 'interesting problems'.

rounds.name: Online assessment
rounds.tests: Coding + SQL + sometimes an API task
rounds.prep: Python for speed. Practice writing working code fast over clever code.

rounds.name: Decomposition
rounds.tests: A vague real-world problem with undefined scope (chess game, parking garage, disease spread)
rounds.scoring: Whether you CLARIFY BEFORE BUILDING — subproblem boundaries and edge cases
rounds.prep: Practice asking scoping questions out loud before writing anything.

rounds.name: Re-engineering
rounds.tests: Find and fix a bug in 500–1000 lines of unfamiliar code
rounds.scoring: Explicitly NOT speed — whether your search process explains why nothing else broke
rounds.prep: Ask what the intended behaviour is before reading. Narrate the search.

rounds.name: Learning
rounds.tests: An unfamiliar system/API with minimal docs
rounds.scoring: Building a mental model from little information; hypothesis testing
rounds.prep: Narrate understanding, uncertainties and your testing plan aloud.

rounds.name: Coding
rounds.tests: Medium/hard DS&A — plus ~20 min of behavioral
rounds.scoring: The behavioral portion is SCORED, not a warm-up
rounds.prep: Have stories ready in this round, not just algorithms.

rounds.name: Hiring manager final
rounds.tests: Project deep-dive, mission alignment, biggest failure
rounds.scoring: 'Missionaries rather than mercenaries'; exact metrics on your own projects
rounds.prep: Know your numbers cold. Have a real failure with what you learned.

questions.note: No public question data for this company. That is expected for companies that do not run LeetCode-style rounds — work the format intel above instead.

stories.story: The retention win that wasn't real
stories.prompt: Tell me about a time you challenged something your team already believed.
stories.situation: At Aleph Lab, a 4-engineer YC startup, a recent push had produced a reported retention gain, and roadmap planning was starting to build on it.
stories.task: Rather than build on the number, I wanted to verify it first — if it was wrong, everything downstream would be wrong with it.
stories.action: I built a Python multi-agent tool on the Claude Agent SDK that mined production data through read-only MCP, so the analysis could never touch live systems, and reconstructed the result from raw production data rather than the existing reporting.
stories.result: The reported gain turned out to be a measurement artifact. I surfaced the real churn drivers instead, and the team reshaped its roadmap around those.

stories.prompt: Walk me through the hardest bug you've debugged. How did you find it?
stories.situation: Aleph Lab's notification pipeline was failing silently in production. Nothing alerted, and the failure was invisible from inside the product.
stories.task: Find out why notifications were not being delivered, and restore the pipeline.
stories.action: I traced backwards from the delivery failures rather than guessing at causes, and found a JWT signing-key migration: the pipeline was still authenticating with a key that was no longer valid, so every request was being rejected. The migration itself was correct — nothing downstream had been updated to follow it.
stories.result: The pipeline went from failing with 401 to healthy at 200. The instructive part was that the symptom (no notifications) and the cause (an auth key rotation) lived in completely different parts of the system.

stories.prompt: Tell me about a problem you found that nobody asked you to look for.
stories.situation: I had shipped a production retention system at Aleph Lab — targeted push via Supabase, Deno edge functions and FCM, with a treatment/holdout A/B.
stories.task: It worked, but nobody had asked whether it was actually reaching everyone it was supposed to reach. I wanted to know.
stories.action: I validated the win-back targeting against live production data and found the logic identifying eligible users was wrong, so a large share of the intended audience was never being reached at all. I corrected how eligibility was determined.
stories.result: Reachable users expanded roughly 2.7×, and the system recovered churned users back into paying subscribers.

stories.story: Making the agent something other teams could actually use
stories.prompt: Tell me about something you built for other engineers rather than for users.
stories.situation: Aleph Lab had a production AI agent that only worked inside our own application. Other teams wanted it, but there was no way to embed it.
stories.task: Turn it into something another team could drop into their app without needing to understand our internals.
stories.action: I packaged it as a typed SDK with versioned APIs and wrote 136 automated tests. I treated the test suite as the contract: if the package was genuinely self-contained, someone with no context should be able to integrate it from the types alone.
stories.result: A new AI coding agent integrated it into a fresh app on the first attempt — the clearest evidence the abstraction actually held, since it had no context to fall back on.

stories.story: Interpreting in a high-security, multi-agency environment
stories.prompt: Why this kind of work? / Tell me about somewhere the stakes were real.
stories.situation: I served as a Military Interpreter for the ROK Army's Capital Defense Command for 18 months, in high-security multi-agency settings with international stakeholders.
stories.task: Provide real-time English–Korean interpretation and translate sensitive documents and briefings, where an imprecise word changes what a partner organisation believes it agreed to.
stories.action: I worked in real time with no chance to revise, across organisations that each used their own vocabulary, and had to carry exact meaning rather than a good approximation of it.
stories.result: Coordination held across government and defense teams. It is the clearest experience I have of work where being loosely right is not a smaller version of being right — and it's a large part of why deployed, consequential software interests me.

stories.story: Owning one layer of a three-person engine
stories.prompt: Tell me about a technical project you're proud of.
stories.situation: Mini Minecraft was a from-scratch voxel engine in C++ and OpenGL built by a team of three. I owned world generation and the render pipeline; chunk streaming and player physics belonged to my teammates.
stories.task: Build a world that read as varied rather than noisy, and a renderer that made it legible.
stories.action: I built 7-biome procedural generation with Perlin, FBM and Voronoi noise using smoothstep blending, carved 3D Perlin-noise caves, and wrote the GLSL render pipeline — PCF shadow mapping, screen-space reflections, vertex ambient occlusion, a day-night cycle, and post-process water and lava overlays through a framebuffer pass.
stories.result: A coherent world where generation and lighting reinforced each other. Building inside someone else's streaming system also forced my generation to be correct at chunk boundaries, not just in isolation.
